item.title: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
item.description:
Report warns attacks on critical infrastructure could lead to demand for retaliation and expose EU divisions

Russian sabotage attacks on Europe are increasing and a “mass-casualty event” is now possible as increasingly skilled operatives target critical infrastructure with ever more complex methods, a leading strategic thinktank has said.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report that Russian intelligence services and their proxies were targeting European railways, energy networks and defence industries in an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine.

item.title: A bakery, a playground, a speaker’s corner … how a former Brussels car garage tore up the art gallery rulebook
item.description:
Repurposing a space previously used for selling Citroëns, the Belgian capital now has its first ever dedicated space for contemporary art. It’s certainly ambitious – but will they be able to fill it?

‘A cathedral of cars” is how the colossal Citroën garage in Brussels was described when it opened in 1934, conceived as a startling glass temple to showcase the streamlined wonders of the automobile age. It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night.

Almost a century later, arts and culture have replaced cars as the great urban consumables of our age. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. The original Parisian Pompidou was designed as a transformable cultural machine for the city; this place takes those urban ambitions to an even greater extreme.

item.title: French town divided over church bells ringing every 15 minutes at night
item.description:
Longtime residents of La Garnache defeat newer neighbours in latest rural culture clash over ‘sensory heritage’

A ding-dong has divided the town of La Garnache in western France over attempts to silence the bells of the local church, which strike all night.

Since 1942, the clock tower of Notre-Dame de l’Assomption has chimed an eighteenth-century hymn every 15 minutes … day and night. Between 10pm and 7am, the bells ring 37 times, adding up to more than 700 individual chimes.
